cues.text: A Courtier's Comfortable Start
Born around 1080 at Xanten , on the Rhine, into a family connected to Germany’s imperial house, Norbert was ordained a subdeacon and given a comfortable canonry.
He later served at the courts of the Archbishop of Cologne and Emperor Henry V , becoming the emperor’s almoner.
This privileged life initially left little room for serious spiritual ambition.
A Dramatic Conversion
Tradition holds that Norbert's decisive turn toward holiness came after he was thrown from his horse during a violent thunderstorm and narrowly escaped death.
Echoing St. Paul's conversion on the road to Damascus, the experience led him to abandon his courtly career, seek ordination as a priest, and give away his considerable possessions to the poor.
An Itinerant Penitential Preacher
Norbert spent several years as a barefoot, itinerant preacher of penance across Hainault, Brabant, and the region of Liège.
His sermons, reinforced by his visibly austere manner of life, drew large crowds.
He reconciled feuding parties and persuaded usurers to make restitution for their ill-gotten gains.
Founding Prémontré
In 1120, guided by a vision confirming the suitability of the Rule of St. Augustine, Norbert settled with a small band of followers at a marshy valley called Prémontré .
Near Laon in northern France, he founded a new community of canons regular that combined the contemplative and active life.
Its members lived under vows in common, yet also served as parish clergy among the laity, a genuinely new middle path between the cloister and ordinary diocesan life.
Archbishop of Magdeburg
Norbert's reputation for reforming zeal led to his appointment in 1126 as Archbishop of Magdeburg , a see on Germany's eastern frontier.
There, he worked to correct clerical abuses and defend Church property against secular encroachment, facing considerable resistance.
Clergy resentful of his reforms even mounted an assassination attempt.
Legacy
Norbert died at Magdeburg on June 6, 1134, and was canonized in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII.
The Premonstratensians , or Norbertines, that he founded spread rapidly across Europe within his own lifetime, reaching from Ireland to the Holy Land.

They remain today one of the most enduring expressions of the twelfth-century canonical reform movement—a religious life built, as the Catholic Encyclopedia observed, to bring 'the religious life into the family circle' of the wider Christian world.
